newsitem.title: USA: U.S. managed futures funds eye other markets.
newsitem.headline: U.S. managed futures funds eye other markets.

text.p: Managed futures funds are increasingly eyeing other markets besides exchange-traded futures and options, to the extent that the Managed Futures Association (MFA) is considering changing its name to recognize the trend, several MFA officials said.
A strategic task force at the six-year-old trade group, as part of a review into hedge funds, for the last month has been discussing changing the name to the Managed Funds Association.

"They (the task force) want to review hedge funds. Are hedge funds' needs similar to our needs, and does the agenda of MFA address the needs of both hedge funds and managed futures?" said John Frawley, MFA chairman and CEO of Merrill Lynch Investment Partners Inc.
Frawley spoke at an MFA luncheon at the start of the MFA's three-day conference on Sunday in Palm Beach.
Hedge funds trade on- and off-exchange products and often use futures and options in their strategies.

Managed futures funds, which must be registered with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission as commodity trading advisers (CTAs), are only allowed by the CFTC to trade futures and options contracts at registered U.S. exchanges. But they can trade other markets if they gain appropriate registration from other U.S. regulatory agencies.
MFA industry officials acknowledge that more CTAs are following the footsteps of Louis Bacon and Paul Tudor Jones, two hedge funds that started out as CTAs, in seeking out cash markets worldwide.
"Our own people are going into hedge funds," MFA's executive director Jane Martin said in an interview. "Hedge funds trade everything, but many of our CTAs are trading off-exchange products."

Hedge funds, which 20 years ago had been primarily in cash stock and bond markets, have broadened their opportunities into the international markets and use strategies with futures and options, said George Crapple, who sits on MFA's task force committee and who runs the Millburn Corp, a hedge fund based in New York City.
"There has definitely been a movement to a common middle ground," Crapple told reporters, referring to trends in both hedge funds and managed futures funds.

While assets in hedge funds and managed futures funds have grown in the last seven years, CTAs' assets in 1996 were $26 billion, according to Managed Accounts Reports Inc, while assets in hedge funds were nearly eight times as much at $200 billion, according to Hedge Fund Research Inc.

Robert Easton, CEO of Commodites Corp Ltd and head of the MFA's task force, said in his address to the conference that a shift in the MFA's agenda was critical since asset growth in managed futures has plateaued since 1994, while growth in U.S. mutual funds has surged.

"If we view ourselves solely as managed futures industry we may never rise to this plateau, but if we follow the evolution of many of our most prominent managers who invest in equities and other cash markets, we too can rebound," Easton said.
Easton's task force will make recommendations to the board on April 23. Recommendations are likely to include consolidating the MFA's offices in Washington D.C. and Palo Alto, Calif., he said.
